title: 2027-06-11 Quantization technical review - AetherTech
topics: Quantization tradeoffs (INT8 vs FP8 vs GPTQ vs AWQ)
summary: Redwood SE walked AetherTech through quantization options for their 7B chat model. Discussed accuracy regressions (common in 4-bit/GPTQ), AWQ promising for stability, FP8 as middle ground, and INT8 performance/cost benefits. Covered runtime tradeoffs (latency vs throughput), KV cache behavior with quantized weights, batching strategies, and VPC/on-prem deployment prerequisites. Agreed next steps: run targeted quant evals, share AWQ/GPQT benchmark spreadsheets, and schedule a pilot VPC deployment.
next_steps: Jordan to share AWQ vs GPTQ benchmark spreadsheet and security pack (link) by 2027-06-13

header:
Date: 2027-06-11
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (AetherTech ML), Ravi Kapoor (AetherTech Infra), Elena Morales (AetherTech CTO)
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're on for about an hour, Jordan from Redwood, Priya our quantization/serving SE, and on the Aether side Maya, Ravi, Elena. Quick agenda: go over INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ tradeoffs, show runtime numbers, talk KV cache and batching, then next steps.
[00:18] Maya: Thanks, Jordan. We are mainly worried about quality regressions after quantization — we have a finetuned 7B chat model, can't take a big drop on generation fidelity. Also we need to run inside our VPC for compliance.
[00:30] Priya: Totally — that's exactly the use-case we've seen. Quick high-level: INT8 gives great perf and smaller memory but can induce more outliers in LLM weights, FP8 is a softer compression that usually preserves more numeric range, GPTQ (post-training quant) is model-aware and often yields better accuracy at 3/4-bit, AWQ (adaptive weight quant) is newer and can give GPTQ-like accuracy with faster runtime.
[01:05] Ravi: Can you explain the latency implications? We care about p95 latency for chat.
[01:12] Priya: Sure. Two axes: per-token computation and KV cache costs. For INT8 and AWQ-optimized kernels, throughput per GPU improves significantly — more tokens/sec. But if your latency SLO is tight (p95 < 200ms) smaller batch sizes matter; INT8 kernels sometimes have less numerical stability requiring extra rescaling which adds small overhead. FP8 tends to sit in the middle: slightly slower than INT8 but better stability — fewer fallbacks. GPTQ 4-bit gives very small memory/latency but can cost you on perplexity for certain prompts; AWQ often recovers accuracy while keeping runtime close to INT8.
[01:55] Elena: Is AWQ production-ready? We've seen mixed messaging.
[02:00] Priya: It's increasingly stable. Our internal tests show AWQ with blockwise reordering + mixed FP/INT fallback reduces token-level MRR drop to under 1.5% on our 7B finetuned set, compared to 3-4% for naive 4-bit GPTQ in some workloads. But results vary by finetune and task. We'll run the exact sweep on your checkpoint.
[02:32] Jordan: Quick note about KV cache — when you quantize weights, KV cache layout doesn't change, but the way attention matmuls are done might shift memory bandwidth patterns. For example, some INT8 kernels require dequantizing for the matmul which increases transient memory and can hurt latency for small batch sizes. That interacts with batching logic.
[02:58] Ravi: So does caching still help as much if we go INT8 or AWQ?
[03:03] Priya: Yes, KV cache still gives the same algorithmic benefit — less recomputation. But effective throughput gain from the cache can be slightly lower if dequantization adds overhead at each step. For AWQ and tuned INT8 kernels that support fused dequantize+matmul, overhead is minimal.
[03:25] Maya: On accuracy regressions — you mentioned mitigation strategies. What are the practical levers?
[03:30] Priya: Several: per-layer quantization granularity (per-channel vs per-tensor), mixed-precision (keep norm/ln in FP16/FP32), activation calibration with representative prompts, GPTQ per-channel optimization, fine-tuning with quantization-aware training (QAT) if you can afford it, and template-aware prompt eval to detect regressions. AWQ's adaptive blockwise scheme helps on outlier layers.
[03:58] Elena: QAT sounds expensive. We can't re-finetune heavy.
[04:02] Priya: Understood. In our experience for a 7B finetuned model, GPTQ or AWQ post-training with per-channel scaling and keeping layernorm in FP16 gives a good accuracy/perf sweet spot without full QAT. We'll test and report delta on your eval set so you can decide.
[04:20] Jordan: Also important: toolchain and kernel maturity. We can do a pilot on Redwood Dedicated or on your VPC private deployment — Redwood's runtime has optimized fused kernels for AWQ/INT8 on Ampere+ and newer, which mitigates a lot of overhead.
[04:37] Ravi: About VPC/on-prem: what's required from our side? Firewall, tenancy, storage?
[04:42] Jordan: We'll need network access for control plane onboarding, initial kube manifests or orchestration hooks if on-prem, and KMS setup if you want customer-managed keys. For air-gapped, there's an on-prem bundle. The quant runtime itself is delivered as container images and native kernel packages; we can pre-validate those in your staging.
[05:02] Maya: How does batching affect latency/throughput in quantized runs?
[05:06] Priya: Batching increases throughput (tokens/s) because you amortize KV reads and matmuls, but increases tail latency. With quantized kernels, batching can be even more effective since memory bandwidth is lower. However, if your user pattern is many single-turn chats, we recommend micro-batching + prefetching KV cache and async response streaming to keep p95 tight.
[05:34] Elena: Any examples of numbers? ballpark improvement % for INT8/AWQ vs FP16?
[05:38] Priya: On a 7B model on an A100/RTX8000 class GPU: INT8 optimized path showed ~1.6-2.2x tokens/sec vs FP16 in our tests depending on sequence length and batch. AWQ tends to be 1.4-1.8x but with smaller accuracy delta. GPTQ 4-bit sometimes gives 2.5x+ in mem reduction and 2.0-2.8x tokens/sec but at the cost of higher variance in accuracy.
[06:10] Ravi: For us latency p95 with chat history of ~200 tokens is around 320ms today; we need to get under 250ms. Any recommendations?
[06:18] Priya: Strategies: reduce batch size (single or micro batch), enable fused kernels for dequantize+matmul, use KV cache warmup, and prefer AWQ or tuned INT8 kernels because naive GPTQ may add dequantization overhead. Also check sequence lengths — truncation and prompt engineering to reduce avg tokens help a lot. We can run a tailored benchmark with your traffic pattern.
[06:45] Jordan: We'll also instrument token-level latency on the pilot so you see the delta p50/p95/p99; Redwood Console can break down time spent in dequant, matmul, KV lookup, and I/O.
[06:56] Maya: About regressions: are there classes of prompts where quantization fails more — e.g., math, code, long context?
[07:02] Priya: Yes. Numerically sensitive tasks like arithmetic or long-context retrieval may show bigger degradation, especially if the model relies on subtle weight differences. Code generation sometimes sensitive too. We'll run focused tests on your prompt categories: support prompts, code-gen, retrieval-augmented queries.
[07:22] Elena: If we see degradation, can we do hybrid routing? Some requests to FP16 vs quantized?
[07:28] Jordan: Absolutely. Redwood supports routing policies: you can route high-confidence or latency-tolerant requests to FP16 instances and high-volume, latency-sensitive ones to quantized instances. Canary rollouts and percentage-based routing are also available.
[07:40] Ravi: For KV cache, is there any difference in storage format that affects persistence across restarts?
[07:46] Priya: No, KV cache serialization is independent of weight quantization. The cache stores activations/keys/values as FP16/FP32 tensors (depending on config) to preserve precision. So persistence across restarts behaves same.
[07:58] Maya: Any gotchas for on-prem drivers or kernel versions?
[08:02] Priya: Yes, kernel compatibility matters. AWQ/INT8 fused kernels rely on CUDA >= 12.x and specific cuBLAS/cuDNN versions for best perf. On older GPUs or older drivers, perf can drop and fallbacks may trigger. We'll validate your node images during the pilot.
[08:20] Elena: Let's talk success criteria — what should we measure in the pilot?
[08:24] Jordan: Suggested success metrics: token-level perplexity or MRR delta <= 1.5% vs FP16 baseline on your eval set, p95 latency under 250ms for typical sessions, and at least 1.5x tokens/sec improvement or 40% cost reduction on inference.
[08:40] Maya: Sounds reasonable.
[08:42] Priya: We'll document the exact eval harness and thresholds in the spreadsheet. We'll also add per-prompt failure examples to help triage.
[08:52] Jordan: Next steps recap — Jordan to send AWQ/GPTQ benchmark sheet + security docs; Priya to run the quant evals on your checkpoint; schedule VPC pilot next week.
[09:02] Elena: Thanks, team. Any immediate blockers from our side?
[09:05] Maya: We'll get the checkpoint and prompts uploaded, and approve a small staging VPC.
[09:10] Jordan: Great. We'll follow up with invites and the shared sheet link: https://redwood.app/sheets/quant-bench-aethertech (internal link).
[09:20] Ravi: One more quick question — licensing for kernel packages for on-prem?
[09:24] Jordan: There is a runtime bundle license for on-prem deployments, standard enterprise terms. We'll include that in the security/compliance pack.
[09:30] Elena: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[09:34] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll send notes and action items.
[09:38] (call ends)
